passage:
I'm Nazia, and this is about my second-year attendance. In the first month I checked the college portal every week. Then I missed a few mornings because of the late bus, and the number turned orange. After that I just stopped logging in.
Bidisha kept asking, "Have you checked?" and I'd say, "It's fine, I'll make it up." Not looking felt so much lighter. Every time I thought about the portal, I opened something else instead.
In October a notice came: students below the limit could not sit the exams without a hearing. My name was on the list. When I finally looked, the number was red, far worse than orange.
I got through the hearing, just. But if I'd looked in August, a few extra mornings would have fixed it.

qa.q: What colour did Nazia's attendance number turn after the missed mornings?
qa.a: The number turned orange, and later it was red.

qa.q: Why did not looking feel lighter to Nazia?
qa.a: Avoiding the portal spared Nazia the bad feeling of seeing the number, so each time it gave a short burst of relief, even as the problem kept growing.

qa.q: What could Nazia have done in August?
qa.a: Keep checking the portal weekly, maybe with Bidisha, and make up the missed mornings early while a few extra days could still fix it.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel seeing Nazia's name on the list?
qa.a: Bidisha might feel sad and a little frustrated, having asked again and again, and also wish Nazia had let a friend help sooner.

grounding: It shows a young adult who stops checking attendance once it looks bad, gaining short relief while the problem grows.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
Pooja, a second-year student, came in today about sleep, but it came out that she hasn't opened her bank messages for two months. It started when she saw a charge she didn't understand. After that, every time her phone buzzed with the bank's name, she swiped it away. "If I don't see it, I can breathe," she said.
Meanwhile small charges kept stacking up, and now her card has been blocked in the canteen.
We opened the messages together here, slowly. She shook at first, then steadied. The total was smaller than she had feared, but some of it needs sorting with the bank. She agreed to call her mother tonight and visit the branch with her on Saturday.
Plan: short check-in next week, and a fixed time each Sunday when she reads her messages.
Vasudha

qa.q: What happened to Pooja's card in the canteen?
qa.a: Her card has been blocked in the canteen.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep swiping away the bank's messages?
qa.a: Seeing them brought fear about the charges, so swiping them away gave a moment of relief, as she said, "If I don't see it, I can breathe."

qa.q: What steps did Vasudha set up with Pooja, and why do they help?
qa.a: Opening the messages together, calling her mother and visiting the branch, and a fixed Sunday time for checking; together they turn a scary pile into small, shared, regular steps.

qa.q: How might Pooja's mother feel when she gets the call tonight?
qa.a: She may feel worried at first, but probably also glad Pooja told her and relieved it is being sorted now rather than later.

grounding: It shows a young adult who stops opening bank messages after bad news, feeling short relief while small problems grow into bigger trouble.

Jasleen found me sulking and made me open the drawer. We read all three together on her bed. It's bad but not impossible. I'm calling Papa tomorrow morning and asking to pay it off in two parts.
Next time a notice comes, I open it the same day. With chai, maybe. 😅

passage: The government college in Hosur put attendance on the notice board outside the office every Monday. In August, Deepak's name was in yellow: 71 percent. He'd been missing early lectures to help at his uncle's tyre shop. After that, Deepak took the side stairs on Mondays, the ones that avoided the board. It felt better not knowing. When Mahima asked, "Did you see the list?", Deepak said, "Yeah, yeah, it's fine." By October the office sent a letter home: attendance too low to sit the semester exams without the principal's approval. His mother read it out in the kitchen, her voice shaking. Deepak remembered August, when a few weeks of mornings would have fixed it.

passage: Siddharth, you've stopped opening the college portal since your attendance dropped, haven't you? Let your Gautam mama tell you something. At twenty, in Hyderabad, I had a small loan for my hostel fees. One month I paid late, and the bank sent a letter. I didn't open it. Then another came. I put them in my suitcase, under my sweaters, and felt lighter every time I zipped it shut. Six months later, the warden called me in: the late fees had grown, and the bank had written to my father. My father came on the overnight bus, sat with me, and we opened every envelope together. The first letter asked for a small amount. The last one was frightening. The problem was never the first letter, beta. It was the suitcase.

qa.a: In Gautam's suitcase, under the sweaters.

qa.q: Why did young Gautam feel lighter each time he zipped the suitcase shut?
qa.a: Gautam felt a quick relief from not facing the bad news, even though the problem was quietly growing inside the suitcase.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mama's story, and what does it suggest for Siddharth?
qa.a: Gautam's father sitting with him to open every envelope; for Siddharth, it suggests opening the attendance record now, ideally with someone calm, and talking to the college early.

qa.q: How might Gautam's father have felt on the overnight bus?
qa.a: Gautam's father was probably worried and upset, yet came to sit beside his son and face it together.

passage: Rashmi knew her attendance in two subjects was slipping after the monsoon floods kept her home for a week. So she stopped logging in to the college portal. No red numbers, no panic. Whenever Nikita asked, "Did you check?", Rashmi said, "Later." Then, three days before the semester exams, the hall tickets came out. Hers was blocked. Accounting: 62 percent, below the limit. The office said she needed a leave letter signed by the head of department, and the HOD was at a conference until the day before the exam. Rashmi sat on the corridor floor, hands shaking. Nikita crouched beside her. "Okay. We email the HOD tonight with your flood photos, and go to the office first thing tomorrow." If she had checked in August, it would have been one easy letter. Now it was a race.

qa.q: What was Rashmi's attendance in Accounting?
qa.a: It was 62 percent, below the limit.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi stop logging in to the portal?
qa.a: Rashmi felt anxious about the slipping numbers, and not looking gave a short relief from the panic.

qa.q: What did Nikita suggest, and what could Rashmi do earlier next time?
qa.a: Emailing the HOD with the flood photos that night and going to the office in the morning; next time she could check the portal regularly and ask for a letter as soon as she's absent.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel crouching beside Rashmi?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt worried and protective, wanting to turn the panic into a plan.

grounding: Shows a student avoiding her attendance records once they looked bad, letting a small fixable problem grow into a crisis.

passage: Bidisha had stopped opening her bank's messages in October, right after the balance dipped below what she needed for rent in her Salt Lake flatshare. The notifications stacked up: 12, 23, 31 unread. Each time she swiped them away, she felt a small, sweet relief. Then, in December, her phone went dead mid-call. The bill hadn't been paid; the automatic payment had bounced twice. Her flatmate Tenzin found her staring at the screen. "How many messages haven't you opened?" "Thirty-one." Tenzin sat down. "Let's open them together. Just read. No panic." It took an hour. There were two bounce charges, a late fee, and one small refund she hadn't known about. "It's fixable," Tenzin said. "Tomorrow we call the bank and ask what your options are." Bidisha nodded, feeling lighter than she had in weeks.

qa.q: How many unread bank messages did Bidisha have?
qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: Why did swiping away the notifications feel good to Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha felt a small, sweet relief each time, because not looking kept the worry about rent out of sight for a moment.

qa.q: What did Tenzin suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Opening the messages together calmly and calling the bank tomorrow to ask about options, which turns a pile of dread into specific, fixable items.

qa.q: How did Tenzin approach Bidisha's problem?
qa.a: Tenzin stayed calm, sat down beside Bidisha, and made it a shared task instead of a lecture.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding bank messages once things looked bad, letting small charges grow until a friend helps her face them.

passage:
In my second year of college, I stopped opening the messages from my bank. It started when I saw my balance was lower than I'd thought. After that, every buzz felt like a small punch, so I swiped them away unread.

For two months that felt fine. Then my phone recharge failed at the station, and my hostel fee payment bounced. My friend Omkar had to lend me money for the bus.

That night I opened forty-three unread messages. Most were small things: a late fee, a subscription I'd forgotten, a charge I didn't recognise. None of them were huge on their own. Together they were a mess.

I'm Bhavna. The next morning I went to the bank with my father and asked the help desk to explain everything.

qa.a: Bhavna opened forty-three unread messages.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna swipe away the bank messages?
qa.a: Every buzz felt like a small punch, so ignoring them brought short relief from the anxious feeling.

qa.a: Omkar might feel concerned for Bhavna and glad to help, but also puzzled about how things got so tangled.

Devika's roommate Kunal came to me today, worried. He said Devika had stopped opening her college email since exams started and had turned off notifications from the fee portal. "She says she'll deal with it after exams," he told me.

When I met Devika, she said she felt sick every time she saw the inbox, so it was easier not to look. Meanwhile three reminders about a scholarship form had gone unanswered. The deadline is Friday.

I sat with her and opened the inbox together. She was shaking at first, then calmer once she saw only the form was urgent. We filled it in there and then, and I've booked her a meeting with the student welfare office tomorrow.

passage:
Since his father's knee operation, Anirban had been running the family's small hardware shop in Bolpur. The supplier bills came in yellow envelopes. At first he opened them. Then, as the numbers got bigger, he started sliding them unopened into the drawer under the counter.
Every time he pushed one in, he felt lighter for a moment. Out of sight.
Trisha, who ran the tailoring shop next door, noticed the drawer wouldn't close. "How many are in there?"
"I don't know," he admitted.
"That's worse than any number," she said. "My uncle does the accounts for half the shops on this road. He's free on Sunday. Bring the drawer."
On Sunday they spread the envelopes across her uncle's table. It was bad, but not as bad as Anirban had feared, and two suppliers had offered a discount for paying early, which he'd missed only because he hadn't opened them.

qa.q: Where did Anirban put the unopened bills?
qa.a: Anirban slid them unopened into the drawer under the counter.

qa.q: Why did Anirban stop opening the yellow envelopes?
qa.a: Anirban felt anxious as the numbers grew, and pushing them away gave a brief feeling of relief.

qa.q: What did Trisha suggest, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: Bringing the drawer to her uncle, who does the accounts for many shops, so someone qualified could help sort the bills.

qa.q: How does Trisha see the drawer that won't close?
qa.a: Trisha sees it as a warning sign and thinks not knowing is worse than any number.

grounding: Shows a young adult who stops opening bills once they look bad, letting problems grow, until a neighbour brings in help.

passage:
By the time the Christmas markets opened in Berlin, Santiago had forty-three unread messages from his bank. He had muted them in October, after one said his account was slightly overdrawn. Muting felt like opening a window in a hot room.
He did the same with the university portal. He missed two statistics lectures, then five, then stopped checking how many.
Zeynep, his flatmate, found a red envelope in the hallway with his name on it. "Santi, this looks official."
"Later," he said, and slid it under a pile of flyers.
Two weeks later an email arrived that he couldn't mute: he was below the attendance limit and could not sit the statistics exam. The bank letter, when Zeynep finally made him open it, showed small fees that had kept stacking up on the overdraft.
He sat on the kitchen floor. "It was small in October," he said.

qa.q: How many unread messages from his bank did Santiago have?
qa.a: Forty-three.

qa.q: Why did muting the bank messages feel good to Santiago?
qa.a: It gave him quick relief, like opening a window in a hot room, so he didn't have to face the worry of the overdraft.

qa.q: What could Santiago do now?
qa.a: He could open everything with Zeynep beside him, then talk to the bank and to a university student adviser about the fees and the exam.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeynep to watch this happen?
qa.a: Zeynep is worried enough to hand over the envelope and later make him open the letter, and probably feels uneasy watching small problems pile up.

grounding: Shows a young adult who stops opening bank messages and attendance records once things look bad, letting small problems grow.
